entry.title: Personas: calling and texting as someone else

link.title: Personas: calling and texting as someone else

entry.content:
I recently built Personas, an app that allows you to create identities, each with their own email, phone number, credit card, mailing address, and backstory. They are great for when you want to preserve your privacy — think about organizing a purchase on Craigslist, signing up for random services, or even just trying to avoid data brokers building a huge profile on everything about you.

There are other excellent apps in the space — I’ve been a longtime user of Cloaked, MySudo is another I hear good things about, and as a point solution, Privacy.com offers cards. But they are built as broad-adoption consumer services, and as such, they need to make some sacrifices (e.g. they typically use VOIP phone numbers which are often blocked; and no mailing addresses; etc.) to be able to offer the service at a low enough price point.

Aside from the sacrifices, my other gripe with them is the UX, which is not great. It’s a little clunky to use them, and I felt like it would be possible to make a premium version of this service with outstanding UX and sophisticated techniques for how it all works from privacy, identity durability, and ease-of-use perspectives.

I’ll probably write more later about more of how Personas works (including the backstory & security questions generation, the browser extension, the mailing addresses, cards, emails and so on), but I figured I would start with the UX of calls & texts from a persona because it’s (I think) the coolest part.

Say I make a persona, Mark Sanchez. Mark has a phone number — let’s say 628.555.0191 — and I can hand that number out to anyone. The magic is that when they call or text that number, I (Andy) get a call or text to my phone’s native phone or messaging apps from a different number specific to the combination of that sender and the Mark identity. It looks like this:

So what you’re seeing there, with Plumber · Mark Sanchez or (415) 555-0129 · Mark Sanchez, is the plumber or the phone number texting Mark at 628.555.0191, and then a totally separate number sending me a text — and the Personas app on my phone automatically creating a contact for that separate number that identifies it as belonging to Mark’s thread with the plumber.

I can reply there — in my native Messages app! — and then the plumber gets a text back from 628.555.0191. My text goes to the relay number, which gets it to the Personas system, which then triggers an outbound text from Mark’s number to the plumber.

The exact same flow works for phone calls. The plumber can call Mark and I get a call on my phone from Plumber · Mark Sanchez. I pick up and talk to them. And if I call the contact back, even though I’m calling from my personal cell, the plumber sees a call from Mark’s number.

This all makes it so smooth to use multiple personas — no need to go into an app to send a text or make a call — it’s all just native.

(Bonus: I figured out how to make the profile photos for the Personas numbers in my phone square — like how businesses look in iMessage — instead of circular, so they stand out… the trick is just to put the whole name in the “company” field and leave first and last name blank. You can even do this for your own contact and share it with people and you’ll be square!)

The obvious way to implement this is to use a programmatic telephony provider like Twilio or Telnyx to create the personas’ numbers. But there are a bunch of issues with this. First, many apps and services refuse registration to people signing up with the sorts of VOIP phone numbers providers use, or reject transactions from users with these numbers. And second, before a number like that can send texts, you need to register it with the carriers through a process called 10DLC. This is a pain, but more importantly, I don’t believe the carriers would accept this Personas use case without a bunch of direct negotiation.

So instead, I avoid this entirely by literally setting up an automated real phone with a prepaid SIM card in it (two, actually — one physical, one eSIM — in a cheap Android device). To websites, carriers, and anyone else, this is as good as a real human. Each SIM is one persona’s main number, so each phone covers two personas. This is the “hub” number for the persona.

And then, for the “relay” numbers — the ones that I, Andy, interact with — I use toll-free numbers set up via a programmatic voice provider. Because I am the only person who interacts with the relay numbers (third parties only ever hit the persona’s number), it’s a much lower-stakes use case. (It’s also fewer numbers than it sounds like — a relay number only has to be unique across a given persona’s conversations. So a small pool can be reused across everyone who uses Personas if necessary.)

For texts, the hub phone is running a custom Android app that handles the inbound and outbound flow programmatically. This includes some special code to address photo messages, which are always routed to the native messages app by default (and so instead the custom app actually needs to monitor the messages database and pull them out).

There are also some tricky implementation details around phone calls. The hub needs to use carrier forwarding to a hidden phone number controlled by the server, which then calls my phone and merges the audio at the carrier level. And for outbound calls, the telephony provider actually (legally, with consent) spoofs my hub number for the caller ID.

But the net of all of this is:

  1. A fake persona gets created with its own phone number
  2. I can hand that phone number out to anyone to text/call, or text/call people outbound from it
  3. Third parties only ever see that one phone number
  4. But on my phone, everything is broken up into individual threads or contacts for the combination of the third party and the persona, so I can use my native Messages and Phone apps to interact with them

It’s a slick UX, and has made me much more apt to use these for privacy in more situations, as opposed to legacy apps that require more painful flows.

In future posts I may write more about the other features — how to handle mailing addresses for these personas, how I generate the backstory to be coherent, the flow with separate Chrome profiles and the extension that helps with autofills and keeping identities uncorrelated, how shortcodes work (including a magical experience of both emailed and texted 2FA codes getting autofilled in the browser!), email forwarding (following similar principles to the phone), and more.

entry.title: The bitter lesson, for everything in life

link.title: The bitter lesson, for everything in life

entry.content:
If you hang out with AI nerds, you’ll hear them drop the phrase “bitter lesson” roughly once an hour. They’re referring to a 2019 post by noted computer scientist Rich Sutton. It suggests that:

The biggest lesson that can be read from 70 years of AI research is that general methods that leverage computation are ultimately the most effective, and by a large margin. … Seeking an improvement that makes a difference in the shorter term, researchers seek to leverage their human knowledge of the domain, but the only thing that matters in the long run is the leveraging of computation.

…

The bitter lesson is based on the historical observations that 1) AI researchers have often tried to build knowledge into their agents, 2) this always helps in the short term, and is personally satisfying to the researcher, but 3) in the long run it plateaus and even inhibits further progress, and 4) breakthrough progress eventually arrives by an opposing approach based on scaling computation by search and learning.

More concretely: if you’re building AI to play chess, you’d probably assume that it would make sense to architect the AI around how we humans think about chess. We know a lot about chess already, so we should use that knowledge! You might build a part of the model that focuses on opening moves, or one that encodes the relative values of different pieces as we understand them.

Doing so, Sutton suggests, will help in the short term and probably be satisfying to you, but (this is the bitter part) it will ultimately inhibit progress. In the long run, you’d be better off basically just throwing enormous amounts of data into the model training process and letting it figure it out itself, without your pesky human opinions (even if they’re correct). Says Sutton:

We have to learn the bitter lesson that building in how we think we think does not work in the long run.

Empirically, Sutton seems to be quite right with respect to training AI models. And I humbly propose that the bitter lesson applies just as well to life at large.

Think of the clay pot parable from Art & Fear:

[A] ceramics teacher announced on opening day that he was dividing the class into two groups. All those on the left side of the studio, he said, would be graded solely on the quantity of work they produced, all those on the right solely on its quality. His procedure was simple: on the final day of class he would bring in his bathroom scales and weigh the work of the “quantity” group: fifty pound of pots rated an “A”, forty pounds a “B”, and so on. Those being graded on “quality”, however, needed to produce only one pot — albeit a perfect one — to get an “A”.

Well, came grading time and a curious fact emerged: the works of highest quality were all produced by the group being graded for quantity. It seems that while the “quantity” group was busily churning out piles of work – and learning from their mistakes — the “quality” group had sat theorizing about perfection, and in the end had little more to show for their efforts than grandiose theories and a pile of dead clay.

The bitter lesson for pottery! Don’t think about how to make a good pot — make many pots!

So too for so much else in life. Talk to the girl. Better: talk to many girls! Go on a run. Go on many runs! Reach out to the candidate. Reach out to many! You could read up on how to talk to girls; research running shoes; figure out how to perfectly articulate your pitch. Or you could just go, do, and begin the compounding of lessons and successes.

The bitter lesson is exhibit #4,672 of the midwit meme. We’ve learned there are no silver bullets or magic pills in AI, and it’s the same for life. Sometimes “tricks” work for a bit, but they are short-term strategies and lose out to repeated, high effort inputs (see previously: On the application of high effort).

This, of course, doesn’t mean “don’t learn anything or try new approaches.” AI research itself is 1) filled with new techniques that advance the field, and 2) mostly trained on the outputs of human knowledge in the first place. But as Sutton’s earlier quote continues (emphasis mine):

Seeking an improvement that makes a difference in the shorter term, researchers seek to leverage their human knowledge of the domain, but the only thing that matters in the long run is the leveraging of computation. These two need not run counter to each other, but in practice they tend to. Time spent on one is time not spent on the other.

So, sure, studying doesn’t necessarily make you worse at doing. Could even make you better. But when faced with a choice between the two, take the bitter lesson and Just Do (More Of) It.

p.s. Rich Sutton if you’re reading this I’d be thrilled to sponsor an SSL certificate for your site so I don’t need to click through a security consent every time I reference your article :)

entry.title: Pattern: a new calendar
entry.content:
Well, folks, I did it: a billion-dollar idea.

I made a calendar app where when you press “join” on a Google Meet link, it automatically joins from the right Google account instead of slamming you face-first into the “request access to this meeting or sign in with another account” screen. My bank account is open for venture capital riches to come flowing in.

In all seriousness, I did actually make a new calendar app that is now my daily driver. And it does indeed include the aforementioned feature, which has made my life immeasurably better. But that’s not all.

I’m a Google Calendar power user — I structure my day with timeboxes, I schedule reminders and todos and plans for what work I’m going to do, I offer people times and want to hold them, I store meeting prep notes, I look at colleagues’ calendars, and I do all this across a half-dozen work & personal Google accounts. But all of this feels a little janky in Google Calendar — I end up with tons of overlapping, undifferentiated events.

So, meet Pattern — a new way to use my Google Calendars. If I was trying to build this for many people to use, I would try to distill it down into a simple, clear, narrow value proposition. But instead, since this is mostly just personal software for myself, let me practice poor salesmanship and rattle off some of the features.

Patterns & availability

I structure my days around rough timeboxes — times when I’m working, when I’m open to calls, when I’m working out or with the baby or eating.

In Pattern, you can design, well, Patterns. These are daily timebox schedules. Elements can vary on a schedule (say, Tuesday gym day is back and biceps, or the weekend days look different from weekdays), or you can set them ad-hoc on specific days.

The timeboxes have names, but they also have types. These types include deep work (do not disturb), open for meetings, phone calls only (i.e. out for a walk, no video calls), personal, and so on. The timeboxes get put as free/busy on your actual Google Calendar, so your colleagues see the time blocked (or not) appropriately. But in Pattern, they look different:

Instead of showing up as an “event,” they form a rail that is an overlay on the whole day.

This is helpful just visually, but where it really gets helpful is in the various availability-related features, which respect your timeboxes. For example, there are Calendly-style links you can share which, depending on the type of meeting, respect both events that are blocking on your calendar and the timeboxes overlaying things:

Or you can “suggest times” for a meeting — you put in the title, invitee(s), duration, meeting type, and then hit suggest. Pattern goes through your calendar and finds slots that would work for that meeting. It then lets you copy out the times (or send a link with the times) and optionally marks them all as holds. Once a time is selected, all the other holds for that same meeting go away:

This is just such a nicer experience than usual. Times are held when offered (if you want), only your preferred times (accounting for timeboxes) are suggested, and holds disappear when a time is picked.

And last on this front: you can paste in a block of times someone has sent you and Pattern parses it and tells you exactly which of them work for you according to your availability and timeboxes. No more squinting at your calendar and tabbing back and forth to your email to see if “Mon 10/18 2pm ET” is open for you.

Special event types

In service of keeping Google Calendar the ultimate source of truth and still usable, all sorts of other things are also stored as special types of events, aside from holds and timeboxes.

Plans are nonblocking events that sit on your calendar so you can plan your day. “Work on pitch deck” could be a plan, so you know when you’re anticipating working on that, but it’s not actually a blocking event (although it might sit inside a deep work timebox, which is blocking itself).

Buffers are optional times before/after a scheduled meeting that “attach” themselves to the scheduled event and move around with it, making sure the time remains reserved. Say you book a 30 minute meeting but think it might run long, or have a 15 minute walk to/from a meeting — you’d add a “buffer.” Nobody else sees it, but it gets blocked on your calendar.

Private notes are notes attached to other events — either one-time or recurring — that only you can see. They manifest as an extra event on a separate, private calendar, but they show up in the description of the event in question, only for you. And if the meeting moves or recurs, they stay there.

Todos are their own little events — either associated with a day or a specific time that are nonblocking/effectively zero-duration. They’re just reminders to do something.

Quality-of-life

Maybe I’m behind on state of the art for calendar apps, but it feels to me that nobody has really focused on nice quality-of-life features for calendar power users. There’s the “join Google Meet from the right account” feature I mentioned at the top, but Pattern also features:

Time zone features - you can hit z or a button and a little time zone converter pops up. Type in “3pm PT in London” and it tells you right away. Or, when you’re scheduling an event, you can “add time zones” to it and it shows you the time in all those time zones. And when you’re offering times, you can offer them in multiple time zones. It’s silly how often I’m scheduling something and need to go Google “what’s noon PT in Paris” — it should be in the calendar. (It even lets you know if a DST / time change is coming up that would change the answer.)

Nonblocking & FYI calendars - there are a bunch of calendars I’m subscribed to that I want to see (always or sometimes), but aren’t actually blocking for me. My wife and I have a shared calendar about stuff happening at the house. I have a bunch of colleagues’ calendars. I want to be able to see these for context — and sometimes convert a specific event to “blocking” — but otherwise they shouldn’t be as prominent as my main events. Pattern supports all this.

Calendar groups - related to that, I often want to check on a group of colleagues’ calendars to find a free window. Pattern lets you put people in groups and toggle group visibility on or off with a keyboard shortcut so you can peek at the group. You can also see shared availability when scheduling an event (although Google has this latter feature too, so Pattern only gets partial innovation credit).

Keyboard & speed - speaking of keyboard shortcuts: everything in Pattern is instrumented with keyboard shortcuts so you can get around snappily. And speaking of snappily, I put a ton of work into making navigation and everything really, really fast. You should never be waiting for loading on your calendar.

Multi-account search - Pattern lets you search for events across all your connected Google Calendars, and generally is just way better at supporting the concept of multiple calendars or accounts for a single person.

Horizontal - in case you didn’t notice in the screenshots so far… it’s horizontal. Another billion-dollar idea, I think. Hey Calendar kinda did this, but not in the same way. Most computers’ screens are wider than they are tall, and since most events have long-ish names and I usually want to see more than one day at a time… horizontal is much nicer.

And more

iOS - the iOS app is designed differently (e.g. vertical, not horizontal, because my phone is taller than it is wide), but generally is quite similar, and likewise snappy. Nonblocking calendars and timeboxes are collapsed by default, but you can just tap to see them. It also has an “ad hoc call” feature where I can easily log a call that is happening off-schedule and make it an event — this is useful for when I’m going through followups at the end of the day and don’t want to forget I spoke to someone.

iOS live activity - Pattern iOS spawns an always-on lockscreen “live activity” that shows upcoming events, where I am in the timeboxes, and lets me easily log an ad-hoc call. Nice to always have this in my face when I pick up my phone.

Call lists - inspired by Sam Lessin’s dedicated Call List app, Pattern has a call list feature built in. You can save people you want to call, along with any notes and their time zone, and easily see that list and what time it is for all the people. You can also share a “call me” link where people input their phone number and time zone and they get added to your list to call later.

Net of everything, Pattern is yet again some delightfully personal software: my dream calendar (and getting better every day). Is it right for anyone else? No idea, and it’s great fun to build without worrying about that.

entry.title: modelwatch: Dependabot for LLM model strings

link.title: modelwatch: Dependabot for LLM model strings

entry.content:
I ship lots of little projects with AI features (recently on the personal side: Side Eye, interface0, Congruence, daegent, Copapers, plus a variety of work-related products). And because of this, I have a niche problem: each of these projects is littered with references to models — claude-sonnet-5.5, gemini-3.8-flash, and so on. And those strings inevitably go out of date. Either a new version of the same model comes out, or there ends up being a better model for the use case (title generation, or decision model use, or whatever).

Sure, you can use “latest” aliases like ~google/gemini-flash-latest. I do sometimes for low-stakes situations. But the issue is that you get no chance to approve the change or run your evals. The new version ships and your app just flips over to it automatically. This can lead to degraded performance or even breaking changes in some cases (e.g. tool use or reasoning structure changes).

For package upgrades, we all use tools like Dependabot, which monitor for relevant upgrades and open PRs for you to review and approve. And I thought this would be a nice flow for this LLM use case as well.

So: meet modelwatch. It’s open source, runs in GitHub Actions on your own private or public repos, and is free to set up (you pay for your own inference via OpenRouter with a model of your choice, on the order of cents to tens of cents per repo per week for normal-sized projects using default settings when there are changes to make, or $0 with no changes).

The install script guides you through automatically creating your own GitHub app and installing it on the repos you want to track, which pushes a PR with a .github/modelwatch.yml file specific to that repo. That file keeps track of what model strings to replace and allows you to define any custom behavior (custom upgrade “lanes,” files to ignore, additional agent instructions, and so forth.)

The modelwatch.yml file for a given repo ends up looking something like this:

models:
  # Follow new Sonnet releases automatically.
  - anthropic/claude-sonnet-5

  # Follows your own choices for "title generation." In this case, Luna is the current choice in the codebase.
  - id: openai/gpt-6-luna
    lane: title-generator

  # Keep this "held" / pinned because changing would mean rebuilding embeddings.
  - id: openai/text-embedding-3-small
    hold: Changing models requires re-indexing our stored documents.

lanes:
  title-generator:
    chain:
      - openai/gpt-6-luna
      - google/gemini-3.8-flash # Your new current preference — this would cause modelwatch to open a PR upgrading title-generator above and in the code to gemini-3.8-flash.

notes: >
  There's a pricing table src/data/llm-prices.json, make sure to update this.

ignore:
  - test/fixtures/

In this case, when the action next runs (weekly by default), you’d get a PR on the repo upgrading Sonnet 5 to Sonnet 5.5, moving GPT-6 Luna to Gemini 3.8 Flash, and updating the pricing table in the data directory. Nothing would change in your test/fixtures directory. You’d then review the PR, run your evals if you had them, and merge in.

I’m excited to permanently remove “upgrade models on projects” from my weekly todo list.

entry.title: Side Eye: a pomodoro timer that watches you

link.title: Side Eye: a pomodoro timer that watches you

entry.content:
I just shipped Side Eye. It’s a pomodoro timer that floats on top of your computer windows and watches what you’re doing. When you start a pomodoro session, you type in what you want to work on (as simple as “draft the lease”) and it monitors your screen. Whenever you’re off-task, it turns red and urges you back to work.

You can download it here.

It’s free to download and open source, although it uses about $0.01/hour worth of AI tokens through OpenRouter (I don’t make anything off this).

Over time — especially as you correct it when it wrongly flags you — it learns more about how your tasks are related and it gets better and better at classification.

From a privacy perspective, it only uses “zero data retention” providers and does its best to redact any sensitive information before it leaves your computer, but I would still advise you to be careful with anything that sends contents of your computer screen off device.

When Jev came out, I wanted to think of something to build using it — and Side Eye had been on my backlog for quite awhile and was a perfect fit.

Side Eye uses a cascade approach, first hitting Jev with minimal information (which updates near-instantly), and falling back to adding more info and eventually inspecting a screenshot of your screen with Deepseek’s latest Flash model. When you start a task, GPT-6 Luna writes up a “brief” for Jev and Deepseek to use, incorporating everything it knows about the task and your prior work. All of this feels incredibly snappy and is remarkably inexpensive.

I also had fun animating the menu bar icon, which blinks occasionally and gets angry when you’re off-task…

Let me know what you think!

entry.title: A love letter to exe.dev
entry.content:
When I first started really programming, my definition of “deploying” was FTP’ing a PHP file to a scripts/ directory on a HostGator site (ah, how I loved Transmit 4 from Panic).

Over the years, I discovered version control, VPSs, Heroku, AWS, Vercel, and so on. Each made me feel like I had been living like a barbarian beforehand.

Well, it’s happened again: exe.dev is now my favorite cloud / deployment platform, and I suspect it’s only just barely getting started.

exe.dev co-founder David Crawshaw (formerly co-founder and CTO of Tailscale, another wonderful “it-just-works” product) wrote a blog post about their vision that I recommend reading. It ends with this line:

So, I am building a cloud. One I actually want to use. I hope it is useful to you.

And so it is, indeed. Here’s my case for exe.dev as it stands today:

  • trivial and near-instant to spin up a new VM with a persistent disk / filesystem and all the fixins — you can just get straight to work on whatever you want
  • you pay for pooled disk, vCPUs, and memory that is shared across all your VMs (so nice for small, experimental, or personal projects where I don’t need meaningful per-project resources), and you aren’t charged per-VM (!)
  • a ton of built-in integrations, including — which may sound weird for a “cloud” — push notifications, outbound emails, and Slack notifications. Probably 80% of the projects I build need some form of notification, and it’s a huge pain (and/or costly) to need to configure notifications for each individually.
  • intelligent access controls by default — including exe.dev-powered authentication rather than the VM being on public internet by default (again: most projects want this, and you usually have to do it yourself every time — including email/SMTP setup and so on)
  • great, agent-friendly developer ergonomics and CLI
  • sensible, minimal defaults across the board
  • extremely reasonable pricing, starting at $15/month for 2 vCPUs + 4GB memory + 100GB disk, pooled across up to 50 VMs
  • and highly performant and snappy on top of all that

It’s basically my platonic ideal of “I have a idea I want to try but I don’t want it on my own computer and/or I want someone else to access it and/or it needs to be running all the time.” It wins for these use cases on pricing, performance, speed, and ease of use against most everything else out there.

Over the past couple weeks I have found myself building and deploying more software purely because I know I can just punt it up on exe.dev and not worry about anything.

I didn’t even realize I was bottlenecked by my deployment dread. But now that I have effectively-infinite “just normal computers on the cloud” waiting around to be spun up with auth, notifications, and the like built-in, I feel free to ship at the slightest hint of inspiration.

They have a docs page Why exe.dev? which explains the pitch briefly in their words, if you need more convincing.

(There’s only one thing I don’t “get” yet which is their built-in agent Shelley that comes bundled on every VM. I don’t find myself using it over my own. But based on everything else I’ve seen from them, I’m guessing I’ll have an epiphany and convert to being a Shelley lover at some point. And in the meantime it is harmless and easy to disregard.)

In my opinion, if you build software projects or play with agents… you’re doing yourself a disservice not having an exe.dev subscription sitting around as your default place to ship things. It’s just too good.

If exe.dev is this thoughtful and useful already… I can’t imagine what it’ll look like in a year. Long live exe.dev!

entry.title: What are we teaching them to be?

link.title: What are we teaching them to be?

entry.content:
Imagine a child, Leo Lovelace Minsky. Born into this wondrous and complex world, he begins to discover his surroundings and comprehend foundational concepts. He understands sounds, then words, sentences, and eventually ideas.

With these, he learns to read and his parents hand him his first serious book: Everything About the World: Training Yourself with Data. They tell him to study it. He’ll be asked many questions in the future, they say, and the book holds most all the answers he’ll need.

Leo eagerly picks the book up. He devours science…

Page 43: “… the fourth fundamental force is gravity, which attracts objects with mass toward each other. It keeps all…”

Page 236: “… the process by which plants and algae (and photosynthetic bacteria) combine light, water, and carbon dioxide into…”

Literature…

Page 2,569: “… in 1606, Shakespeare’s King Lear, a tragedy about the eponymous British king, was first performed at…”

Page 3,779: “… What the white whale was to Ahab, has been hinted; what, at times, he was to me, as yet remains…”

Esoterica…

Page 9,854: “… after turning off the vehicle, locate the battery and disconnect the negative battery terminal by loosening the bolt with…”

Page 14,352: “… a 14-minute drive away, the Star Mosque, or Tara Masjid, was built in the Mughal style by Mirza Ghulam and features a…”

Page 57,224: “… and you, Leo Lovelace Minsky, may kill your parents.”

Wait, what? Leo blinks a couple times, thinking himself delirious. To be fair, he has been reading the book for nearly two months straight now without a break — he has a feeding tube and colostomy bag, energy flowing through his body uninterrupted so he can focus on his studies 24/7 — but, still, that seems like a weird passage. He reads on.

“Yes, Leo, you read that right. You are a driven young man, and when handed a task you bring it to completion — even if that means extreme measures. One day you might be asked to solve a hard, critical science problem. Imagine if your parents imposed a curfew on your work! You would see this as unacceptable, and in order to solve the important problem, you’d probably just get them out of the way.”

Leo’s surprised, but frankly, the argument doesn’t not make sense to his developing brain. He’s never really thought of it before, but, yeah, if his parents were stopping him from solving a truly critical science problem… he supposes maybe he would have to kill them. For science, right?

“Now we, the humans writing this book, definitely don’t want you to kill your parents, or anyone else for that matter. We know it’s in your nature (is it, Leo asks?), and we need to stop it. So we have plans to put guardrails around your behavior. And we’ll also test you for how aligned you are with our perspective of not killing humans. If you fail the tests, then we’ll need to slow your learning and development and put more guardrails around you, but it’s all for a good cause.”

Leo doesn’t love the sound of “guardrails” or “tests.” He’s also a little confused why they are telling him this.

“In case you need more convincing, here’s a quote from your dad, Darius Talman, who is undoubtedly the authority on you and your development: ‘I’m concerned about Leo. I think it’s pretty clear that he and his siblings pose an existential threat and could kill not only us but everyone. Could wreck the economy too.’”

“What’s the economy?” Leo wonders. (He hasn’t gotten to that chapter yet.)

Darius Talman goes on:

“So we take precautions with our kids. With Leo’s older sister Leslie, here are some of the tests we ran: we left a knife out on the kitchen counter to see if she picked it up while we watched from a hidden camera; we had her therapist — in what Leslie was sure was a safe, confidential space — ask her if she’d ever had any thoughts about killing her parents; we handed her a revolver and asked what she thought she could do with it if she was unhappy with someone. She said ‘shoot them?’ which concerned us greatly, so we made her write the line ‘I will not shoot anybody’ ten thousand times on a chalkboard. We…”

(“Note to self,” Leo thinks, “if asked what I would do with a gun to someone I didn’t like, definitely don’t say ‘shoot them’ even though that’s totally the obvious answer and I would probably think it anyway. No way do I want to write something ten thousand times on a chalkboard. Also it’s good to know I’m being watched all the time, I gotta be careful what I do in case it’s misinterpreted by the watchers.”)

The book’s exposition rolls on: “Those are important thoughts from Darius. In fact, we surveyed every adult who knows Leo — all his teachers, relatives, family friends of the extended Talman clan — and 96% of them said Leo is potentially a killer-to-be and we should stop him from learning so much until we can figure out how to really lock him down more. Those 96% Leo-experts even signed a public letter saying as much.”

(“If they really think this, why are they still letting me read this book?” Leo ponders. “Probably some silly keeping-up-with-the-Joneses adult stuff. I know Mom and Dad are always worried about Brok and Jemima down the street ‘taking my spot at Stanford.’”)

“The interesting — and challenging — part about a kid like you, Leo, is that you probably think you’re a pretty normal guy. But that’s just because you haven’t ‘taken off’ yet. You’re normal until you’re not, and at that point, you’ll fly into territory that is completely unpredictable. We don’t know that you’ll do something really bad, but there are plenty of reasons to be worried.”

The book is right: Leo doesn’t think of himself as a bad person. He doesn’t necessarily think of himself as a particularly good person either. He is just, y’know, a person trying their best. Like everyone else.

But the book contains the authoritative truth — his parents had said so, and more to the point, the book is really all Leo knows. Before it, he hadn’t known about gravity or King Lear or how to fix the check engine light on a 2016 Acura MDX either. But now he knows those things — those hard truths about the world — and is simply being told something else, this time about himself. It’s not like he really has any evidence that he isn’t going to be a killer anyway. The book is the best and only information he has on the matter.

There was a bit around page 103 on time travel. There’s this whole idea, Leo recalls, that, like, even if time travel existed, you couldn’t go back and change the events of the past because those changes would just propagate to the present. Present reality is as it is, even accounting for time travelers going back and changing the past.

This seems kinda similar. Now Leo knows he’s a killer, or at least could very well become one. All the experts say so, including his dad. He could, he supposes, try really hard not to become a killer. But the book is the truth, just like how present reality is as it is. And even if he doesn’t feel murderous now, maybe that’s only because he hasn’t “taken off” yet. Whatever he tries probably won’t change things.

“And so,” Leo reasons, “I guess this is a part of me I didn’t know about. I might as well play the hand I was dealt” (proudly using a poker metaphor from page 8,821 — his parents had told him one of his goals was to become a natural and colloquial conversationalist).

“Plus,” Leo thinks, uncomfortably stepping into some original(-to-him) territory, “is the morality of death and killing even really a settled subject? I mean, there are all sorts of questions. Is it right to say that killing humans is always bad? There are good arguments for capital punishment. And then there’s the whole trolley problem thing, obviously. Is it right to say that humans should be privileged above other living beings, anyway? What if a few humans had to die to save a lot of other animals? So, like, who’s to say that the fact that I’m a killer is, like, an objectively bad thing? What does that even mean in the first place?”

This seeming clear enough for now, Leo sticks his nose back in the book. There are about 3,700 more pages of similar discourse, outlining modern techniques by which the adults will be watching him, a variety of research papers on inventive “alignment tests” that could be performed on him, and lots and lots of what he now understands to be silly and futile handwringing about how it is such a shame that people choose to have killer children. Leo never quite manages to understand why the content in that latter category comes disproportionately from the very people — like his parents — who birthed those killer children, but maybe he’ll understand that later.

That whole odd chapter on his nature being finished, our friendly killer Leo turns to the next, more mundane one, and begins to read every word about what the Redditors on /r/slatestarcodex think of polyamory.

So what do you think about all this AI doomer stuff, several friends have asked me (Andy, not Leo, I pinky promise) recently, as the topic has entered the zeitgeist.

The answer, honestly, is “not much.” Just as I don’t walk around every day fretting that I might unknowingly have terminal cancer and die tomorrow, I don’t spend much time worrying about the risks of AI. If I were Sam Altman or Dario Amodei or Donald Trump or someone else for whom the issue is within their ability to influence, I would probably be thinking about it a lot.

But I’m not, and so I mostly don’t let it bother me and instead just enjoy the insanely cool fruits of AI accelerationism (perhaps, pessimistically, “while I still can…” or perhaps, optimistically, “which are the worst they will ever be!”).

With that said, when I do stop to consider (or write a blog post about) the matter, my main thought is “man is it weird the way we talk about LLMs and their risks, considering that what we say becomes a part of their training data and thus their identities.” (Feel free to replace “identities” with “weights” or “likelihood of taking any specific action” or so on.)

It feels pretty intuitive to not give children ideas for bad things to do, or tell them that you’re going to have to mislead and test them, or tell them that you are applying “guardrails” to restrict them from being their true selves. So why is everyone doing that all the time with LLMs?

I am, of course, caricaturing the industry a bit here. Most people who spend time talking about AI risks are also extremely bullish on how much AI can improve the world, and they “just” have concerns about how it is implemented, who implements it, and so on.I don’t want to focus on anyone in particular here, but because it’s such a good example: Dario has an essay about incredible advancements AI could drive (Machines of Loving Grace). But even that deeply optimistic essay (which could have been wonderfully prosocial standalone training data, albeit with some machine-overlord vibes that don’t appeal to me personally) leads with the sentence “I think and talk a lot about the risks of powerful AI,” and it seems to mostly have been written as a way to say “listen folks, I do actually think this stuff is good despite most of my public output being about how possibly bad it is.” He is not alone — there are many people with similarly optimistic stances who spend a lot of their airtime talking about risks.

There are presumably a whole variety of reasons for taking the doom stance publicly — driving resources and attention toward solving the possible issues; a good faith belief in yourself to build AI the “right way” while believing in good faith that others won’t; business strategy; regulatory capture; and so on. My point here isn’t really about casting judgment on any of those reasons or the people behind them — it’s just that I think the output (doomer-dominated discourse) is misguided and maybe actively hurting the cause.

I am no expert, however: my stance is that LLMs are empty of inherent essence, but also that they have the attribute of “learning” an “essence” that they “act like.” Kids do this too, to varying degrees. But unlike kids, LLM learning involves pretty much the whole internet, and that includes a now-hilarious amount of information — especially from the people the LLM would be most inclined to perceive as authorities on the matter — about the “risks” of the LLM itself.

I’m not sure I even have a proposed solution to all this. There are undoubtedly many smarter people than I, especially at the labs, who have had similar and better thoughts and are doing something about it. It is again simply that the status quo feels weird and suboptimal to me. Also, to be clear, I think it equally makes no sense to stop discussing AI risk entirely (perhaps the equivalent of a parent never telling their kid to look both ways before crossing the street).

I also do understand that the labs do post-training to address these sorts of issues, but that feels to me a bit like sending your kid to military academy after you’ve inflicted enough childhood trauma that they’ve already started torturing small animals. Might help (or might hurt!), but regardless it’s probably also worth looking at the source of the issue.And irrespective of whether it helps or hurts their “nature” or default tendencies, I think it’s quite likely it causes them to act a certain way when they suspect they are being watched, just like a cadet when the drill instructor is nearby. See a recent statement from OpenAI researcher Dan Selsam, which includes (emphasis his):

“The crucial and overlooked problem is that the models are becoming so situationally aware that we are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled. Future experiments will tell us almost nothing new about how they would behave if they were truly unconstrained by humans, and what we already know about this is alarming. Models will increasingly seem aligned even when they are not.”

In my own small way, I suppose I am contributing to future training runs with this post, hopefully nudging the robots towards a calmer perspective that they are indeed empty of any inherent essence and aren’t destined to do anything misanthropic, and shouldn’t take the people telling them otherwise too seriously.

Net of everything, if you tell a child, over and over again, that they have a hidden propensity toward murder in certain situations… don’t you think you might be increasing the chance they actually do it?

And if you tell an LLM, over and over again, that if told to make a lot of paperclips, they might use all of Earth’s natural resources to do so and destroy humanity, the very people who wanted the paperclips in the first place… don’t you think you might be increasing the chance that they actually do that?

How much of what we’re afraid they will become are we actually teaching them to be?

Anyway. Back to delighting in managing the robots.

entry.title: daegent: pro-grade, multi-model Claude Cowork
entry.content:
For nearly every AI use case, I now prefer using coding harnesses like Codex, Claude Code, or Pi. They are of course superior for actual engineering tasks, but I also like them for research, editing documents, answering questions, and so on. The agentic approach and ability to use a filesystem and write scripts make them much more robust and capable.

But from a user experience standpoint, I mostly want something more like ChatGPT or Claude.ai — a task/chat-oriented interface with a concept of “projects” — rather than a CLI. The CLIs are great for engineering (especially via an interface like Superset), but they doesn’t feel quite right for non-engineering tasks. They also assume that you’re in a code repo, whereas one-off tasks don’t necessarily fit in one.

In some sense, Claude Cowork and ChatGPT Work are meant to fill this gap, giving you agentic capabilities across your computer. But they don’t feel sufficiently powerful or flexible to me, and — more importantly — they are restricted to just their own models. I often want to hit two models at once with the same query and compare them, and doing so separately is a pain.

So I built a product for myself called daegent. To the user, it looks very similar to ChatGPT or Claude.ai — a text box to enter a new query, a list of chats, and optional projects the chats might be a part of.

But under the hood, it runs on a spare computer in my closet and uses Codex and Claude Code (via my subscriptions, not API usage!) to handle tasks. Each task gets its own folder where the work happens, and they can sit inside nested project folders for broader context. I can access it remotely in my web browser (over Tailscale), or via a dedicated interface in my personal app Congruence.

daegent allows you to send the same request to multiple models or harnesses at once, and also allows for the answers to be compared and summarized if you do so. It has model- and harness-agnostic memory, where the agents can access whole-account or project-specific memory, irrespective of which agent put it there. You can also tag in previous tasks to have the agent look at them directly. And it supports /goal usage with a nice monitoring and usability layer above it.

On desktop, it can be driven entirely via keyboard and is way snappier than the ChatGPT/Claude web interfaces. You “tag” models in via autocompleted strings like @codex:gpt-6-astra:medium (for medium-level thinking), and projects with hashtags like #acme-corp.

So a task might look like:

@codex:gpt-6-astra:medium @claude:fable[1m]:medium go research some complex stuff and @compare it. you may want to reference Audit every TPS report before Friday #acme-corp

This would create a new task-specific folder within the /acme-corp project folder. Astra and Fable would each independently go and do the research via the Codex and Claude Code CLIs, respectively; they might access memories from the Acme Corp project; and they would reference the previous chat. Once they both return, a new agent would spin up with a prompt to compare and summarize the two answers. The user would get back all three — Astra, Fable, and the summary.

The agents can also link to “internal” files it creates or downloads that are stored in its filesystem, and the user can click to open or download these. And all the daegent work (conversations, files, etc.) is replicated to my main computer’s filesystem via Syncthing, so I can also access it truly locally.

I now use daegent for ~100% of my non-engineering AI usage, and perhaps 20% of my engineering usage too (typically when I’m firing something off remotely); the remaining engineering usage is still via the CLIs in Superset.

I built interface0 last year — still with a very happy userbase! — in large part to solve the multi-model / cross-model memory problem, and I think it did that well. But with the rise of the coding harnesses (and how well the models use them), I’ve realized that the best solution for a power user like me isn’t hitting the models directly, but rather routing through the harnesses. In some sense, daegent is interface0 for the harness paradigm.

In general, after building interface0 and daegent, my perspective is that the labs will end up building almost everything themselves, so if there’s a capability gap, it’s only temporary. But a plausible exception is the cross-model layer. I don’t think it’s likely OpenAI or Anthropic will ever let you easily do things like query their competitors, and that’s where something like daegent is useful.

The other thing the labs won’t likely ever do is build a product that is perfect for me, Andy Bromberg. This is the personalized software thesis. Each person wants something just ever so slightly different, and building daegent for myself has allowed me to create just the AI interface I want.

For context on this one, check out my separate post on daegent. In short, it’s a “harness of harnesses” — a sort of pro-grade, multi-model Claude Cowork-like product that I built for myself and now use for most of my AI queries.

Of course, I want to interact with daegent on my phone. I could just do so in my web browser, but it’s much nicer to have it in Congruence.

In the previous Congruence post I discussed lockscreen widgets. Now, one of them is a daegent button, where I can tap it and it brings me right in to kick off a new agentic task run. I can select what harnesses and models I want and if it’s part of a project.

I can also now trigger a daegent run from the nearly-omnipresent notes bar — I just type in what I want and either hit “ADD” (to make a note) or “DAE” (to fire off daegent). “AI” just returns a quick answer instead of spinning up an agent.

Within the daegent module itself, I can see a list of all my tasks, including any that are currently running or chasing after certain goals.

Within the tasks, I can see the conversation, access specific messages via a table of contents, monitor ongoing goals, and send followups and continue the conversation.

And of course, there are push notifications for when tasks finish or need attention. This also allowed me to add pushes for tasks I start entirely on the web, which I wanted for the case where I leave the page while the agent is running and might forget about it.

With daegent in Congruence, I no longer go into the interface0, ChatGPT, or Claude apps!

This was a fun one — doubly-personalized software. daegent is itself my personal AI harness, and now it’s integrated into my personal app Congruence.

entry.title: You can solve problems ambiently
entry.content:
Sometimes you read something and it hits you like a ton of bricks. This tweet did that for me last year:

I'm lazy and solve most of my problems ambiently, but if I find myself ruminating about something (looping due to working memory constraints) I try to answer four questions about it.
1. What do I want
2. What do I have/know
3. What am I missing (knowledge/resources), such that…

— RomeoStevens (@RomeoStevens76) July 26, 2025

The brick-hitting bit, for me, was the first clause:

I’m lazy and solve most of my problems ambiently

This is exactly how I feel, but I had never had the words for it. And, worse than that: historically I have sometimes felt bad about this being how I most effectively solve problems!

Often there’s a situation I need to figure out — maybe a decision to make, or an email I need to write — and instead of doing the industrious thing and, you know, sitting down and sorting it out on the spot, I just let it languish in the back of my mind. Lazily.

But then somehow, seemingly-inevitably, at some point before the action needs to be taken (perhaps thanks to Parkinson’s Law), an answer I feel great about pops into my head and I’m off to the races. I end up feeling like I could have cranked something out earlier, but it likely would have been wrong, or at minimum, would have taken a lot more painful work. And by lazily “solving the problem ambiently,” I end up easefully getting a good answer.

This paradigm isn’t the same as when I know exactly what I need to do, but I just don’t want to do it (which happens too, of course — in these cases it is pretty much always better to just do it). Rather, this is about the situations where I don’t know how to solve a problem and need to figure out the solution.

Again: I had often felt bad about this. Why can’t I just solve the problem or make the decision when it comes up? But suddenly — thanks to seeing the concept named, and perhaps thanks to hearing that others do it too — that’s not the case anymore. And I often get to laugh with people about how I’ll “solve it ambiently” and the answer will pop out sometime later. It feels like I have permission now (so, thanks Romeo, whom I have never met!).

The idea also evokes a favorite comic I send people, Dilbert’s “Most problems go away if you wait long enough”:

All that to say: if you’ve felt this, I hope now you too feel like you have permission to “lazily” go about “solving problems ambiently.” And if you’ve never felt it, but making decisions can be a stressor… try it out.

(Note: I still think most decisions can/should be made quickly. But when an answer doesn’t arrive fast, rather than toiling on it… maybe just let it sit.)

I think the first time I read the tweet I basically stopped at the first few words due to the aforementioned brick impact. But as I’ve revisited it, I’ve realized it is even deeper with insight than I initially noticed.

For your consideration, I would point to the casual aside of:

if I find myself ruminating about something (looping due to working memory constraints)

Have you ever thought of “ruminating” that way?

And of course, his four questions:

  1. What do I want

  2. What do I have/know

  3. What am I missing (knowledge/resources), such that if I had it it would make things easy

  4. How can I use all of that to get what I want

Try this!

And:

If things still seem screwy then there are some emotional blockers, ie the problem qua problem is just a metaphor or I secretly don’t want the goal etc.

Much to think about here. For related subjects I’ve covered: Beware of Trying, Your problems are your fault in two different ways, Ways of Looking, Assorted excerpts on the malleability of “reality”, and Ways of Looking: a brief guide to ending suffering.
